To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) daycare assistance (onsite childcare and childcare service allowances) is found to have a significant positive effect on gender equality in management; (2) PRP is found to have an adverse effect on gender inequality in management; (3) the effect of PRP on gender inequality in the workplace is mediated by the existence of MBO, information sharing, and a formal training system; (4) PRP is more likely to have adverse impact on gender equality if the firm is a large firm

(i) daycare service assistance has a positive effect on the proportion of female core workers and the proportion of women in management; (ii) transition period part time employment results in a decrease in female representation in management; and (iii) PRP has an adverse effect on gender inequality, but this is fully mediated by MBO, information sharing and systematic training.

(i) daycare service assistance has a positive effect on the proportion of female core employees but a negative effect on the proportion female directors, (ii) PRP has a negative effect on gender equality in management (the proportion of female directors) that is fully mediated by a more transparent decision-making process, a more objective performance measurement and evaluation system, and a systematic and formal training program, (iii) the effect of PRP on gender equality in core labor force is fully mediated by the more objective performance
In summary, our research is concerned with

the impact of WLB practices and PRP on gender equality in management and provides evidence that WLB practices can have a positive effect on female representation in management and PRP has a negative effect on gender equality in leadership positions.
the possible effects of specific HRM practices on gender equality in Japan and provides new and important evidence on this issue.
how the HRM practices of individual firms affect gender equality in the Japanese workplace and provides new insights for policy makers and practitioners in Japan and other countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect on gender equality in leadership positions in firms of WLB practices and PRP is mixed and depends on the type of WLB practice, type of PRP, and the mediating role of other HRM practices.
the efficacy of WLB practices in achieving gender equality in the Japanese workplace is not as straightforward as it is often thought to be.
WLB practices are more effective than PRP in achieving the policy objective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

WLB practices that are designed to improve work life balance for women are effective for improving gender equality in management, while PRP is effective in improving firm performance, but may have an adverse impact on gender equality.
the impact of WLB practices and PRP on gender equality in management is not straightforward and depends on the nature and design of specific WLB policies and PRP systems.

WLB practices that are designed to enhance gender equality can be effective in achieving the goal of "womenomics" while the introduction of PRP may have the adverse effect of exacerbating the gender gap in leadership positions in the firm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
policy makers should consider carefully the possible adverse effect of PRPs on gender equality and design public policy instruments to mitigate the adverse effect.
there is no "one size fits all" solution to achieving gender equality in the Japanese workplace.
policy makers should not assume that the introduction of WLB practices and PRP will automatically lead to an improvement of the situation of women in the labor force.
